t.3.31.1: Then the distressed Śūrpaṇakhā, greatly enraged, spoke harsh words in the midst of his ministers to Rāvaṇa, who made the worlds cry out.
t.3.31.2: Heedless amid the pleasures of desire, acting as you please, unrestrained, you do not perceive the terrible danger that has arisen, though it ought to be perceived.
t.3.31.3: A king who is attached to vulgar pleasures, who acts as his desires dictate, and who is greedy, is not highly regarded by his subjects, just as the fire of a cremation ground is not.
t.3.31.4: The king who does not himself attend to his duties at the proper time surely perishes, together with his kingdom and those very affairs.
t.3.31.5: A king who employs no spies, who is hard to gain an audience with, and who is not his own master, people shun from afar, as elephants shun the mud of a river.
t.3.31.6: Those kings who do not protect their realm and are not masters of themselves do not shine forth with prosperity, just as mountains sunk in the ocean do not.
t.3.31.7: Having made enemies of the self-possessed gods, Gandharvas and Dānavas, and being fickle and without spies at work, how will you remain a king?
t.3.31.8: O best of conquerors, those kings whose spies, treasury and policy are not under their own control are no better than common men.
t.3.31.9: Because rulers of men see all matters, even those situated far away, by means of spies, kings are therefore called far-sighted.
t.3.31.10: I think you have no spies at work and are surrounded by common ministers, you who do not realize that your own kinsmen and Janasthāna have been destroyed.
t.3.31.11: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds have been slain by Rāma alone, and Khara too, together with Dūṣaṇa.
t.3.31.12: Rāma, tireless in his deeds, has granted safety to the sages, made the Daṇḍakas secure, and overpowered Janasthāna.
t.3.31.13: But you, Rāvaṇa, are greedy, heedless and dependent on others, you who do not perceive the danger that has arisen in your own realm.
t.3.31.14: A king who is harsh, who gives but little, who is heedless, arrogant and deceitful, no creature runs to aid when calamity befalls him.
t.3.31.16: He does not attend to the tasks that must be done, nor does he fear when dangers arise; soon, fallen from his kingdom and wretched, he will become no better than blades of grass.
t.3.31.15: A king who is excessively proud, unapproachable, self-conceited and prone to anger is struck down in times of calamity even by his own people.
t.3.31.17: There may be some use for dry sticks, for clods of earth, and even for dust, but there can be no use at all for lords of the earth who have fallen from their place.
t.3.31.18: Just as a garment that has been worn, or garlands that have been crushed, are of no further use, so a king who has fallen from his kingdom, even though capable, becomes worthless.
t.3.31.19: The king who is vigilant, all-knowing, master of his senses, grateful, and righteous in conduct, that king endures for a long time.
t.3.31.20: Though asleep with his two eyes, he stays awake with the eye of statecraft; the king whose anger and favour are made manifest is honoured by the people.
t.3.31.21: But you, Rāvaṇa, are foolish and devoid of these qualities, you whose spies did not discover the great slaughter of the Rākṣasas.
t.3.31.22: A king who despises others, is attached to sensual pleasures, does not know the true distinctions of place and time, and whose mind is unfit to judge merits and faults will soon lose his kingdom and perish.
t.3.31.23: Thus Rāvaṇa, lord of the night-roamers, endowed with wealth, pride and strength, reflected with his intellect upon his own faults as she had proclaimed them, and pondered for a long time.
